title: What Is Single Sign-on (SSO)_ How It Works

segments.text: What is SSO or single sign on? Let's take a look. SSO is an authentication scheme.
It enables a user to securely access multiple applications and services using a single ID.
When SSO is integrated into apps like Gmail, Workday or Slack,
it provides a pop-up widget or login page for the same set of credentials.
With SSO, user can access many apps without having the login each time.
SSO is built on a concept called Federated Identity.
It enables sharing of identity information across trusted but independent systems.
There are two common protocols for this authentication process.
Samo or security assertion markup language is an XML-based open standard for exchanging identity information between services.
It is commonly found in the Work environment.
The other common protocol is OpenID Connect.
We should all be familiar with this.
When we use our personal Google account to sign into applications like YouTube,
we are using OpenID Connect.
You use this JWT or JSON web token to share identity information between services.
Now let's walk through a typical SSO login flow and learn how it works.
In this walkthrough, we'll focus on Samo.
An office worker visits an application like Gmail.
In Samo terms, Gmail, in this example, is a service provider.
The Gmail server detects that the user is from a work domain
and returns a Samo authentication request back to the browser.
The browser redirects the user to the identity provider for the company specified in the Samo authentication request.
Octa, all zero and one login are some common examples of commercial identity providers.
The identity provider shows the login page where the user enters the login credentials.
Once the user is authenticated, the identity provider generates a Samo response
and returns that to the browser.
This is called a Samo assertion.
The Samo assertion is a cryptographically signed XML document that contains the information about the user
and what the user can access with the service provider.
The browser forwards the signed Samo assertion to the service provider.
Now the service provider validates that the assertion was signed by the identity provider.
This validation is usually done with public key cryptography.
The service provider returns the protected resource to the browser,
based on what the user is allowed to access as specified in the Samo assertion.
This completes the walkthrough of a basic SSO login flow.
Now let's see what happens when the user navigates to another SSO integrated application.
Say, Workday.
The Workday server, as in the previous example with Gmail,
detects the work domain and sends a Samo authentication request back to the browser.
Now the browser again redirects the user to the identity provider.
The sensor user has already logged in with the identity provider.
It skips the login process.
And instead generates a Samo assertion for Workday,
detailing what the users can access there.
The Samo assertion is returned to the browser and forwarded to Workday.
Workday validates the sign assertion and grants the user access accordingly.
The earlier we mentioned that Open ID Connect is another common protocol.
The Open ID Connect flow is similar to Samo,
but instead of passing sign except mail documents around,
Open ID Connect passes JWT.
JWT is a sign JSON document.
The implementation details are a little bit different,
but the overall concept is the same.
So, which one of these SSL methods should we use?
Both implementation are secure.
For an enterprise environment where it is common to outsource identity management
to a commercial identity platform.
The good news is that many of these platforms provide strong support for both.
So the decision then depends on the application being integrated
and which protocol is easier to integrate with.
If we are writing a new web application,
integrating with some of the more popular Open ID Connect platforms.
Like Google, Facebook, or GitHub is probably a safe bet.
You would like to learn more about system design,
check out our books and free weekly newsletter.
Please subscribe, you will learn something new.
Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
